newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Thai rubber sector has room to expand - Rabobank.
newsitem.headline: Thai rubber sector has room to expand - Rabobank.

text.p: Thailand will reap benefits from the expected continued high price of rubber as unlike the world's other main producers, its production capacity is large, Dutch agri-bank Rabobank said in a report.

Prices are seen remaining high as a result of world capacity limitations but Thailand's replanting programme has left the sector in good shape and better returns have more than offset the impact of rising wages and encouraged further investment.

But the country's supremacy on the world rubber market will come under increasing threat from Indonesia in the next few years unless steps are taken to boost productivity and cut the relatively high costs of rubber tapping.
"Making a move towards the implementation of labour saving tapping techniques looks essential in order to resist Indonesia as a competitor," Rabobank said in a study of Thailand's agribusiness.

Tapping, the process of cutting the bark in a spiral, has to be carried out every other day and is a highly skilled job. But the shortage of rural labour in Thailand has reduced the number of tappers and driven up wage costs.

The bank recommends that farmers investigate alternative methods such as half spiral tapping with the application of a stimulant or the use of motorised tapping knives in improve productivity without driving up costs.
Over 90 percent of Thailand's semi-manufactured rubber is destined for export, amounting in 1995 to around 1.6 million tonnes -- 42 percent of worldwide rubber exports.
International demand relies heavily on the level of economic activity and recession in the major car producing countries can seriously affect rubber exports.
But Rabobank said it expected demand would continue growing in the short term, particularly in Asian countries.

"Continuing "above average' growth is expected in China, Taiwan, South Korea and other Asian NICs (newly industrialised countries), thus creating opportunities for Thai rubber exports," the report said.
But one cloud over the export situation was the burgeoning level of domestic demand.
In a little over ten years domestic consumption has multiplied four-fold and is expected to grow further as more and more processors are integrating forward into the production of rubber products.
The government is offering a variety of incentives to attract foreign investment.
"It is expected that if domestic consumption reaches the targeted 25 percent (of total production), there will be little room for export growth in the next century," Rabobank said.
